source: British Gymnastics — Assistant Foundation Coach Handbook, v.1.0 (April 2026)
note: Content on this page is Chris Sharkey's own paraphrased summary of the BG Handbook for quick reference during coaching. It is not a reproduction of the original document. Always refer to the official BG Handbook and policies on british-gymnastics.org for full detail, definitive wording and the latest updates.

topics.title: The Responsibilities of an Assistant Coach

subtopics.title: Duty of Care
subtopics.summary: Duty of care is a coach's core responsibility: providing safe, inclusive environments that protect everyone from harm and support their physical, emotional and mental welfare. You act 'in loco parentis' — in place of a parent — from the moment a child arrives until they're safely returned.

sections.heading: The Foundations of Duty of Care
points: Five interconnected foundations, all required together: Health & Safety, Safeguarding & Welfare, Equity/Diversity/Inclusion, Interpersonal Relationships, Professional Boundaries.
Everything in the handbook sits under one of these five foundations.

subtopics.title: Health & Safety
subtopics.summary: Practical safety responsibilities: what to wear, how to assess risk, how to move equipment and support gymnasts safely, and how to respond when something goes wrong.

sections.heading: Being prepared to safely coach
points: Clothing: torso fully covered (t-shirt/polo/jumper), long trousers or mid-thigh-to-knee shorts. No loose hoodies or open pockets when demonstrating or supporting. No buckles or clasps.
Footwear: socks minimum for hygiene; clean indoor trainers only if your facility allows. Sliders can be worn moving around but must come off for support/demonstration.
Hair tied back if long. Nails kept short. All jewellery removed when providing manual support — exceptions (new piercings, religious/medical items) must be taped/covered and reported to your Manager.

sections.heading: Risk assessments
points: Formal risk assessments: carried out by Manager/Head Coach/Lead Coach on a scheduled basis and before each session.

Dynamic risk assessment: your continuous, in-session job — watch equipment set-up, space, equipment wear, gymnast wellbeing, and who's in the building. Fix it or report it without delay; you don't need to formally log it, but tell your Lead Coach afterwards.

sections.heading: Manual handling & safe lifting
points: Clear route, get help for heavy/awkward items, keep a clear view, slide rather than lift where possible.
Lifting technique: stable base and firm grip, bend knees with a straight back, heaviest side close to the body, clear path, take your time, never walk backwards.
Gymnasts can help move light equipment if age/strength-appropriate and supervised — never large apparatus (vault, beam, trampoline, DMT).

sections.heading: Safe manual support
points: Three types: Supporting (sustained, weight-bearing contact through most of the skill), Spotting (support only at key moments, e.g. start/landing), Shadowing (following alongside, ready to assist).
Manual support helps with height, rotation, speed, impact reduction and confidence — but weigh it against alternatives (equipment, training aids) since over-use creates dependency.

Best practice: identify the assist point in advance, support close to centre of mass (not limb ends/joints), have a stable base, don't overreach, tell the gymnast what you're doing and why, stay able to move with them.
Never support: front of the neck, chest (between pectorals to mid-rib), above inner mid-thigh, buttocks/intimate areas.
Avoid supporting through joints (wrists, elbows, knees) or by the hand on beam — support closer to centre of mass (hips, under upper arm) instead.
A typical progression away from support: assist in a padded set-up → spot/shadow padded → no assistance padded → assist unpadded → spot/shadow unpadded → independent unpadded.
Accidental contact with an inappropriate site: tell the child it was unintentional, apologise, and inform your Lead Coach, Welfare Officer and the child's parents/carers.

sections.heading: Accident & incident response
points: Accident sequence: stop the activity and make the area safe → don't move the injured person, check consciousness/breathing → report immediately to the Lead Coach → support the First Aider as directed.
Report every accident, however minor, and report near-misses too — both help prevent a future accident.
Know before every session: who the First Aider is, where the kit/phone are, your facility's first aid procedure, and any gymnast-specific medical/allergen needs.

Incidents (fire, missing child, building failure, severe weather, etc.) follow your facility's Emergency Action Plan: stop the session, ensure gymnasts are safe, report immediately, follow directions.

sections.heading: Safe environment — supervision ratios
points: You coach under a Lead Coach (Foundation Coach/Level 2+) who supervises and takes responsibility for you.
Minimum standard: indirect supervision — you can run your own group of up to 8 gymnasts while your Lead Coach observes.
You only coach skills within your own syllabus, unless directly assisting a more qualified coach.
A qualified Helper may directly assist you; an unqualified helper may only support with class/group management (timekeeping, directions, water bottles, behaviour) and moving equipment.
Minimum two responsible adults (18+) in the environment at all times, one being Foundation Coach (or equivalent) qualified or above.

sections.heading: Positive learning practices
points: Physically and mentally prepare gymnasts before new skills.
Confirm prerequisite skills are secure before progressing.
Allow enough repetition/practice time.
Break skills into phases and parts before combining them.

subtopics.title: Safeguarding & Welfare
subtopics.summary: Your legal and moral responsibility to protect children and adults from harm — recognising abuse, responding to disclosures, reporting concerns, and building a safe coaching environment and online presence.

sections.heading: Key definitions
points: Safeguarding: policies, procedures and practices that protect health, wellbeing and human rights.
Welfare: an individual's health, wellbeing and happiness.
Child protection: the part of safeguarding focused on children at risk of, or suffering, significant harm.
A child is anyone under 18 (UNCRC). At 16–17 the term shifts to 'young person' but the same protections apply — including to 16–17 year old coaches themselves.
Coaches are recognised as being in a 'position of trust' (Sexual Offences Act 2003, England & Wales; not covered under Scotland's 2009 Act).

sections.heading: Training & criminal record checks
points: 16–17 year olds: the 'Foundations of Gymnastics Coaching' course covers the requirement; the certificate expires on your 18th birthday regardless of when it was awarded.

18+: must complete a tutor-led Safeguarding and Protecting Children course (gymnastics-specific UK Coaching course in England/Wales/NI); valid 3 years. Scotland requires the Child Wellbeing and Protection in Sport course at any age.
Criminal record check required regardless of age, renewed every 3 years: DBS (England/Wales/IoM/Channel Islands/Gibraltar), Access NI (Northern Ireland), PVG scheme membership (Scotland).

sections.heading: Who to go to
points: Club Welfare Officer — your first point of contact for any concern (unless it's an emergency).
Lead Coach — report to them if the Welfare Officer isn't available.
Regional Welfare Officer — extra support if neither of the above is available.
BG Welfare & Safe Sport Team — 0345 129 7129, welfareandsafesport@british-gymnastics.org, if you feel none of the above are the right fit for a specific concern.

sections.heading: Recognising signs of abuse
points: Five recognised types: Emotional, Physical, Sexual, Bullying, Neglect.
Poor practice (e.g. bad stretching technique, favouritism, inappropriate jokes) is different from abuse but should be reported the same way — it can escalate if ignored.
Vulnerabilities that increase risk: SEND, poor home environment, being looked-after, LGBTQIA+ identity and how others perceive it.
You may notice a concern by hearing something, seeing something, being told something, or simply having a feeling something isn't right (contextual safeguarding) — all are valid reasons to report.

sections.heading: Responding to a disclosure
points: Do: stay calm, listen without interrupting, focus only on them, tell them you must inform the Welfare Officer, reassure them it's not their fault, keep questions to a minimum.

Don't: keep it to yourself, dismiss it, show shock/judgement, panic, probe for details, promise secrecy, decide yourself whether abuse occurred, approach the accused, investigate, or badmouth the accused.
Immediate danger: report to your Lead Coach without delay inside the gym environment (they contact police); call 999 yourself if outside the environment.
Record what was said in the child's own words as soon as possible, and share only with the Welfare Officer.
Confidentiality: safeguarding information must only be shared with your Lead Coach or Welfare Officer — never with colleagues, friends or other parents, however good your intentions.

sections.heading: Embedding safeguarding in practice
points: Always coach in an open, visible area with a minimum of two responsible adults present.
Physical contact: high-fives/thumbs-up over hugs for celebrating; an arm around the shoulder rather than a full hug if a gymnast initiates one.
No intimate care (toileting, changing) — that's for parents/carers, or an approved carer for additional-needs gymnasts.
No entering changing rooms while gymnasts are present.
Give gymnasts a voice — actively ask for feedback on sessions.
No favouritism, no intimate relationships with gymnasts, no travelling alone with gymnasts.

Room sharing while away: 16–17 y/o coaches can share only with other 16–17 y/o coaches, never with a gymnast or an over-18 coach. 18+ coaches never share with anyone under 18. A parent/registered carer may share with their own child.

sections.heading: Online & digital conduct
points: Decline friend requests from any under-18; no gaming/social contact with any child regardless of club membership.
Photos/videos for training only on a club device, kept in the gym and stored securely — never on personal devices.
Under-18 coaches must not control club social media accounts; only staff/parents get access.
No posting gymnast photos/video without consent; messaging apps with gymnasts must always include the Lead Coach/Welfare Officer and parents, and training-related only.

sections.heading: Safeguarding adults
points: Legal definitions of 'adult at risk' vary by nation (Care Act 2014 England; Social Services & Wellbeing Act 2014 Wales; Adult Support & Protection Act 2007 Scotland; Adult Safeguarding Prevention & Protection Policy 2015 NI).
Adults can also experience financial, domestic, organisational, modern slavery and discriminatory abuse alongside the categories seen in children.

Respect an adult's right to choice: if they disclose but don't want it reported and aren't in danger, encourage them to report it themselves. Immediate danger overrides consent — call 999/Adult Services and inform them you have done so.

subtopics.title: Equity, Diversity & Inclusion
subtopics.summary: Creating environments where everyone gets fair, non-discriminatory opportunities to take part and feels they belong.

sections.heading: Core definitions
points: Equality: same, fair, non-discriminatory opportunities for everyone.
Equity: recognising people need different levels/types of support to access the same opportunity — equity should be your minimum standard, not equality alone.
Diversity: recognising and valuing differences in background, identity and experience.
Inclusion: making sure everyone feels welcome and can take part without barriers.

sections.heading: Equality Act 2010 — protected characteristics
points: Age, gender reassignment, marriage/civil partnership, pregnancy/maternity, disability, race, religious belief, sex, sexual orientation.
Doesn't apply in full to Northern Ireland (disability is covered separately under the Disability Discrimination Act 1995).

sections.heading: Types of discrimination
points: Direct: treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic.
Associative: less favourable treatment because of association with someone who has a protected characteristic.
By perception: judging ability based on assumptions/beliefs, not fact.
Indirect: a rule applied to everyone that disadvantages someone with a protected characteristic.
Harassment: offensive behaviour targeting a characteristic, even if not aimed directly at the person.
Victimisation: unfavourable treatment because someone made or supported a discrimination complaint.
Subtle Acts of Exclusion (SAEs): small, often unintentional words/actions that exclude — e.g. touching a gymnast's hair, mispronouncing names repeatedly, assuming ability based on disability.

sections.heading: Embedding EDI in practice
points: Get to know each gymnast individually; show compassion when they share something about themselves.
Give everyone equal time/opportunity and a chance to give feedback.
Adapt delivery to individual needs (equity, not one-size-fits-all).
Use inclusive language — ask pronouns and preferred names, avoid gendered group terms like 'guys'.
Be aware of religious/cultural needs (jewellery, uniform, prayer, fasting).
Model inclusive behaviour and challenge stereotypes; reflect regularly on your own practice, ideally with an observer's feedback.

subtopics.title: Interpersonal Relationships
subtopics.summary: The connections you build with gymnasts, coaches, welfare officers and parents/carers, underpinned by trust, respect and consistency.

sections.heading: Core skills
points: Effective communication: non-verbal communication carries the most weight, then tone of voice, then the words themselves.
Empathy: seeing the situation from someone else's perspective, non-judgementally, and communicating that you understand.
Active listening: full attention, no interrupting or finishing sentences, reflect back what you heard.

sections.heading: Top tips
points: Use names, ask open questions, listen more than you talk, be curious, smile, use a positive tone, open body language, eye contact, be non-judgemental, don't interrupt.

sections.heading: Coach–gymnast relationship building
points: Session start: greet by name, ask how their day was, recall details from last time.
During: give them a voice, notice and ask about their reactions to activities, praise effort/teamwork/creativity as well as technique.
End: give them a chance to reflect and feel positive — they should be able to answer 'How was your session?' well.

subtopics.title: Professional Boundaries
subtopics.summary: The BG Standards of Conduct and Standards of Deployment that govern your behaviour as a coach.

sections.heading: Standards of Conduct — key never-dos
points: No smoking; no alcohol during or in excess before any activity.
Never use offensive language/gestures, jokes, nicknames or derogatory comments.
Never flirt, make sexual advances or touch unnecessarily.
Never allow malicious gossip or discriminate directly/indirectly.
Never have participants on personal social media, or post offensive content on professional accounts.
Never misrepresent your accreditation or poach gymnasts from other clubs.
Never discuss a gymnast's performance where you could be overheard at an event.

sections.heading: Standards of Deployment — legal requirements
points: Criminal record check (DBS/PVG), Safeguarding & Protecting Children certificate (age/nation dependent).
Home Nation membership, insurance (usually via membership), commitment to policies/procedures and CPD.

sections.heading: Data protection
points: Sensitive personal data (name, address, contact, medical) never leaves the gymnastics environment — locked cabinet or password-protected club device only.
Report any lost/misplaced/shared sensitive data (a 'data breach') to your Welfare Officer/Lead Coach immediately.

subtopics.title: Continued Professional Development
subtopics.summary: Your responsibility to keep learning throughout your coaching career.

sections.heading: CPD activities
points: BG/partner coach education courses, online CPD modules, workshops/webinars/conferences, podcasts/articles/books, mentor discussions, peer observation (both directions), Communities of Practice.

sections.heading: Building a CPD plan
points: 1) Evaluate & reflect on strengths/gaps, confidence areas, goals and feedback received.
2) Prioritise development areas and identify suitable activities.
3) Set specific goals with a 'when'.
4) Be present — prepare beforehand, engage during, consolidate after.
5) Record and reflect — keep dates, certificates and notes on impact.

subtopics.title: Physical Literacy & Positive Gymnastics Experiences
subtopics.summary: Physical Literacy is a person's ongoing relationship with movement — a mix of enjoyment, confidence, competence, and understanding of the benefits. It's the strongest driver of whether someone stays active for life.

sections.heading: How to develop it
points: Understand the gymnast in front of you — observe, ask, give them a voice.
Design activities and delivery around what you've learned about them.
Build knowledge, understanding and passion for the sport and their body.
Seek feedback and adapt collaboratively — talk openly about what's working.

subtopics.title: Growth & Maturation
subtopics.summary: Chronological age doesn't predict physical, biological or psychological development — gymnasts of the same age can differ by several years across these. Misreading this is a major cause of injury and drop-out.

sections.heading: Four types of 'age'
points: Chronological: birth-certificate age.
Physical: height/stature-based age.
Biological: hormonal/physical maturity stage.
Psychological: social, emotional and cognitive maturity.

sections.heading: Typical puberty windows
points: Males: late childhood 6–8, pre-puberty 9–11, early puberty 12–14, late puberty 15–18, post-pubertal 19–20.
Females: late childhood 6–8, pre-puberty 8–10, early puberty 10–13, late puberty 13–15, post-pubertal 15–20.
Growth spurts (approx. males 5–12cm over 12–18yrs, females 5–9cm over 10–15yrs) can temporarily disrupt balance, spatial awareness and cause joint aches — be ready to adapt activities.

sections.heading: What to do with this
points: Vary apparatus/activity heights within a same-age group — physical age varies widely.
Expect mood swings, tiredness and inconsistent presentation from gymnasts starting puberty — react with flexibility, not frustration.
Psychological maturity doesn't track physical/biological maturity — give choice, encourage two-way communication, praise effort not just success, check in regularly.

subtopics.title: Being an Inclusive Coach
subtopics.summary: Removing barriers to participation — physical, emotional, social or mental — so every gymnast can take part and thrive.

sections.heading: STEP model for reasonable adjustments
points: Space: can everyone access the environment as set up?
Task: how will each gymnast do the activity — what would help?
Equipment: what pieces would help each gymnast succeed?
People: who around you can offer extra support?

sections.heading: Activity Inclusion Model (AIM)
points: Open: everyone does the same activity, minimal adaptation.
Parallel: group split by ability, same activity on two different set-ups.
Modified: same activity, adapted for individual needs.
Specific: a gymnast practises a component separately before rejoining the group (e.g. handstand alone before handstand forward roll).

sections.heading: Being an EDI advocate day to day
points: Give gymnasts a voice in the support they receive — ask, don't assume.
Mix communication methods (verbal, visual, written, non-verbal); address at eye level; check understanding; allow extra response time; reduce distractions; use consistent routines.
Consider alternative communication (Makaton, BSL, symbols, assistive tech) where useful.
Notice signs of anxiety/overwhelm and respond with reassurance, calmer environment or space to process.

subtopics.title: Holistic Development
subtopics.summary: Developing the whole person, not just technical skill — across Physical, Emotional, Cognitive and Social domains.

sections.heading: The four domains
points: Physical: fine/gross motor skills, coordination, spatial awareness, fundamental movement patterns.
Emotional: allow expression of feelings, talk about them, encourage regulation.
Cognitive: encourage exploration and appropriate problem-solving challenge.
Social: allow play, encourage communication, reinforce positive relationships.
Underpinning all four: know and understand your gymnasts — who they are, what they enjoy, their growth/maturation status.

subtopics.title: Fundamental Movement Patterns
subtopics.summary: The building-block movement competencies (grouped as ABCs, RJT, CKPs, Flexibility, KBGs) that underpin safe gymnastics skill development.

sections.heading: ABCs
points: Agility — changing body position quickly with control (e.g. stuck-in-the-mud, chassés, direction-change leaps).
Balance — keeping centre of mass over base of support, static (headstand, one-foot stand) or dynamic (spins, leg kicks).
Coordination — using two+ body parts together smoothly (choreography, hand apparatus while moving).
Speed — how fast you can move a body part (run-ups, relays).

sections.heading: RJT
points: Running — has a flight phase (unlike walking); vault/tumbling/DMT run-ups.
Jumping — take-off, flight, landing; for height or distance.
Throwing — propelling an object for height, distance or accuracy, under/overarm.

sections.heading: CKPs
points: Catching, Kicking, Passing — controlling and directing objects with hands or feet.

sections.heading: Flexibility & KBGs
points: Flexibility: range of movement around a joint (pike walks, bridge rocks, splits).
Kinaesthetic sense: body awareness and relationship between body parts.
Gliding: moving smoothly and continuously (chassés, linked leaps).
Buoyancy: floating ability (water-based, not developed in a gym session).
Striking with an implement: bat/racket/stick control.

subtopics.title: Keeping it Fun!
subtopics.summary: Fun is the biggest driver of long-term participation — and it looks different at different ages.

sections.heading: What fun looks like
points: Smiling, relaxed posture, laughter; chatty and encouraging; creative and experimenting; energetic, asking for 'one more go'; resilient about mistakes.
5–8yrs: instruction-based games (Simon Says); may enjoy the coach joining in.
9–12yrs: competitive/challenge activities, relays, teamwork tasks.
Teens/adults: creative, self-directed use of previously learned skills.

subtopics.title: Anatomy & Physiology
subtopics.summary: The skeletal and muscular systems are the two most directly relevant to coaching decisions — what bones/joints/muscles are involved in a movement, and how they grow and adapt.

sections.heading: Types of bone
points: Long (movement, e.g. humerus), Flat (organ protection, e.g. skull), Short (strength/stability, e.g. carpals/tarsals), Sesamoid (protects tendons, e.g. patella), Irregular (attachment points, e.g. vertebrae).

sections.heading: Bone growth & the growth plate
points: The whole skeleton is replaced roughly every 7–10 years via ossification (cartilage → bone) and remodelling (osteoclasts break down, osteoblasts build).
Weight-bearing exercise increases bone density — but too much load on growing bones can damage growth (epiphyseal) plates.

If muscle strength outpaces skeletal strength, injuries like Osgood-Schlatter's (a common adolescent knee injury) can result — a key reason to match load to stage of maturation, not just chronological age.

sections.heading: Joints
points: Fixed/fibrous (no movement, e.g. skull), Slightly-moveable/cartilaginous (e.g. vertebral column), Freely-moveable/synovial (e.g. knee, shoulder, hip).

Synovial joint types: Pivot (rotation — neck/forearm), Hinge (flexion/extension — knee/elbow/ankle), Saddle (thumb base), Ball & Socket (all directions — shoulder/hip), Condyloid (multi-directional — wrist), Plane (small gliding — between metacarpals).

sections.heading: Movement vocabulary
points: Rotation, Flexion, Extension, Adduction (towards midline), Abduction (away from midline), Circumduction, Plantar flexion (pointing toes), Dorsiflexion (flexing feet), Pronation (palm down), Supination (palm up), Depression (moving downward).

sections.heading: Muscular system
points: Three muscle types: Smooth (involuntary, internal organs), Cardiac (involuntary, heart only), Skeletal (voluntary, 600+ muscles, attach to bone via tendons — the ones you're coaching).
Antagonistic pairs: as the agonist contracts, the antagonist lengthens. Fixators stabilise the joint; synergists fine-tune the movement.
Contraction types: Concentric (muscle shortens), Eccentric (muscle lengthens under tension), Isometric (no change in length, e.g. holding a plank).

sections.heading: Key muscles & their action
points: Pectorals — adduct arm/shoulder. Deltoids — move arm at shoulder. Trapezius — controls shoulder girdle. Latissimus dorsi — adducts/extends arm. Biceps — flexes forearm. Triceps — extends forearm/arm.

Abdominals — rotate/raise trunk. Obliques — twist/side-bend. Hip flexor — flexes hip, lifts knee. Gluteals — abduct/extend hip. Quadriceps — flex hip, extend knee. Hamstrings — extend hip, flex knee. Gastrocnemius — flexes knee, points toes. Tibialis anterior — dorsiflexes ankle.

subtopics.title: Biomechanics
subtopics.summary: The forces acting on, within and produced by the body during movement. Understanding it sharpens your coaching points, error-spotting and feedback.

sections.heading: Energy
points: Kinetic energy: energy of motion (depends on mass and speed).
Elastic potential energy: stored in stretched/squashed material — springboard, trampoline bed, air track — released back into the gymnast.
Gravitational potential energy: stored by height; converts to kinetic energy on the way down.

sections.heading: Forces, Centre of Mass & Base of Support
points: Balanced forces = no change in motion (standing still); unbalanced forces create, stop or redirect movement.
Centre of Mass: the point mass is equally distributed around — roughly just behind the belly button standing tall, but it moves with the body and can sit outside it.
Base of Support: any point(s) of contact with a surface.

sections.heading: Planes & axes
points: Frontal axis + Sagittal plane (divides left/right) — e.g. forward roll, headstand.
Sagittal axis + Frontal plane (divides front/back) — e.g. cartwheel.
Vertical axis + Transverse plane (divides top/bottom) — e.g. log roll, spin on one foot.

sections.heading: Static skill stability
points: Centre of Mass must stay above the Base of Support in line with gravity.
Bigger Base of Support = more stable (e.g. headstand's 3 points of contact); lowering Centre of Mass adds further stability.
Smaller Base of Support (e.g. one foot) needs the Centre of Mass moved precisely over it — may require shifting the whole body or extending limbs.
Raising the arms overhead raises and moves the Centre of Mass further from the Base of Support, reducing stability.

sections.heading: Dynamic skills
points: Travelling requires deliberately moving the Centre of Mass outside the Base of Support in the travel direction — controlled instability.

Rotation (forward/backward/sideways) needs the Centre of Mass kept continually moving away from the Base of Support (momentum); it stops rotating once Centre of Mass sits back above the Base of Support.
Twisting rotates around the vertical axis — initiated by torque (moving limbs in contact with apparatus) or tilt (shortening one side of the body).
Flight path/parabola: leaning further forward on take-off (>45°) trades height for distance (flatter, longer curve); leaning less (<45°) trades distance for height (tighter, higher curve).

subtopics.title: Session Preparation
subtopics.summary: Everything before the session starts — knowing the plan, arriving early, helping set up.

sections.heading: Your responsibility
points: Know the plan and goals before you start.
Arrive early to help set up apparatus and complete risk assessments.
You may be asked to design activities — get the group, age, level, ability, goals and equipment clarified with your Lead Coach first, and share your plan before the session.

subtopics.title: Session Introduction
subtopics.summary: Setting the tone as gymnasts arrive — roughly 2–3 minutes of a 60-minute session.

sections.heading: What it includes
points: Welcome gymnasts by name, register, visual readiness check (clothing safety, done subtly).
Check in — how are they, any injuries/tiredness/hydration/mood that might need adaptations.
Introduce the session goals and any new coaches/gymnasts.
Parent questions about their own child's readiness: make time. Other topics: redirect to your club's usual process.

subtopics.title: Warm-Up
subtopics.summary: Raises heart rate/body temperature and mobilises joints/muscles. Roughly 10 minutes of a 60-minute session.

sections.heading: Three parts
points: Pulse raiser: fun, inclusive, everyone active — competitive/cooperative/command-style game, may prime fundamental movement patterns for the session ahead.
Mobility: controlled, self-directed movement of the joints/muscles to be used — mobilising, not stretching for flexibility.
Muscle activation: fundamental or gymnastics-specific movement patterns, prerequisites, basic shapes — should prepare, not tire (this isn't conditioning).

subtopics.title: Gymnastic Activities
subtopics.summary: The main part of the session — roughly 40–45 minutes of a 60-minute session.

sections.heading: What to keep in mind
points: Duty of care: risk-assess continuously, keep every gymnast in view, only use trained support techniques, stay within your syllabus.
Whole-person focus: adapt activities to build competence/confidence, avoid queuing, use partner work and hand apparatus.
Consciously apply the BG Coaching Skills and Coaching Styles.
Progress skills safely using your technical understanding, and bring genuine warmth and encouragement.

subtopics.title: Cool-Down
subtopics.summary: Returns heart rate/temperature to resting, helps clear lactic acid. Roughly 5–10 minutes.

sections.heading: What it includes
points: Light cardiovascular movement plus stretching relevant to muscles/joints used in the session.
Stretches should be slow, gentle, self-directed — returning muscles to resting length, not developing flexibility.
Keep it engaging (music, story, hand apparatus, gymnast choice) so the session finishes 'on a high'.

subtopics.title: Session Conclusion & Ending the Session
subtopics.summary: Reviewing the session, gathering feedback, safely dispersing gymnasts, tidying up and reflecting — usually under 5 minutes for the conclusion itself.

sections.heading: Session conclusion
points: Evaluate and reflect with gymnasts against the session goals — everyone should leave with a sense of pride.
Gather feedback: what did you enjoy and why? What would you like more of? What would you change?
Use positive reinforcement — praise effort, persistence, courage, teamwork, not just technical progress.
Finish with a positive non-verbal gesture (high-five/thumbs-up) — the aim is that every gymnast can answer 'How was your session?' well when a parent asks.

sections.heading: Dispersal, tidy-up & reflection
points: Gymnast dispersal: help gymnasts gather belongings and hand them to a known parent/carer under Lead Coach supervision; if collection is late, wait inside with the gymnast and inform your Lead Coach.
Tidy up equipment safely, following Lead Coach direction.
Session evaluation & reflection: consider what went well, what you'd change, and feed this into your CPD.

subtopics.title: Technical Terminology
subtopics.summary: The shared vocabulary for talking about how a skill is built and taught.

sections.heading: Core terms
points: Prerequisite: the shapes/movements/skills a gymnast must already be competent at before starting a new skill (e.g. straight body shape, weight through arms, body tension, one-foot balance — before a handstand).
Technique: how the biomechanics of the movement determine what the body needs to do (e.g. converting forward into upward momentum on vault).
Coaching points: what the gymnast should try to do, based on technique (e.g. 'feet forward, shoulders back' for a hurdle step onto springboard).
Phases of a skill: the start/middle/end moments of a skill, each with its own biomechanics (e.g. a straight jump = preparation, in the air, landing).
Progression: a linear sequence of activities that develop a phase or part of a skill.
Adaptation: changing how an activity is done, or the activity itself, to suit the gymnast.
Physical preparation: fitness-component activities (strength, balance, speed, flexibility) that support the skill — distinct from progressions.

subtopics.title: Physical Preparation for Assistant Coaches
subtopics.summary: Selecting activities that build the fitness components a skill needs, safely and appropriately for the gymnast's stage of development.

sections.heading: General vs specific
points: General physical preparation: fitness foundations — gross movements (running, jumping, landing, lunging, balancing, hopping, squatting, bear walking), low–medium intensity, medium–high volume.
Specific physical preparation: targets a particular skill/movement (e.g. handstand hops before a vault handspring).

sections.heading: Components of fitness
points: Cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, strength, flexibility, balance, agility, coordination, power, speed, reaction time.

sections.heading: Training targets by component
points: Strength: 85–100% effort (7–10/10 perceived exertion), 2–6 sets of 1–5 reps, 2–4 min rest.
Speed: 70–85% effort, 1–3 reps, short/high-intensity with a 1:4 work:recovery ratio.
Muscular endurance: 20–70% effort, 12+ reps, 3–5 sets, short rest.
Flexibility: self-directed methods only for Assistant Coaches (per BG Flexibility Training Policy); hold 15–60 seconds, up to 4 times.

sections.heading: SPORT principles of training
points: Specificity — relevant to the sport/skill/goal.
Progressive — gradually increase intensity/duration.
Overload — load must exceed what the body is used to, to adapt.
Reversibility — fitness declines if training stops or reduces.
Tedium/variety — vary training to prevent boredom and overuse injury.

subtopics.title: Skill Development Considerations & Optimal Challenge
subtopics.summary: Balancing challenge so gymnasts stay motivated and safe — not bored, not scared.

sections.heading: The optimal challenge continuum
points: Over-challenged: activity too hard — low confidence, fearful, low success rate (<6/10). On high-risk activities this is a safety issue, not just a motivation one.
Under-challenged: activity too easy — disengagement, boredom, a leading cause of drop-out (10/10 repeatedly = time to increase difficulty).
Optimally challenged: ~6–8/10 success rate — the sweet spot for learning. Still needs praise and feedback, and needs monitoring as it shifts.

sections.heading: General principles
points: Build competence and confidence with relevant progressions, physical preparation and positive feedback.
Don't rush — define what 'consistency' looks like and require it across several sessions before progressing.
Continually adapt activities to keep every gymnast in the optimal zone.

subtopics.title: The Principles & Processes of Safe Skill Development
subtopics.summary: A four-step process for planning how to teach any skill safely.

sections.heading: The four steps
points: 1) Understand the skill: prerequisites, technique, phases, coaching points.
2) Understand how to progress it technically: choose progressions and physical preparation.
3) Consider how to progress it safely: safe apparatus/equipment use, safe manual support techniques, individual gymnast needs, and what 'success'/'consistency' looks like.
4) Consider how to make learning it enjoyable: organisation, coaching style, how gymnasts will practise, which coaching skills you'll use to keep it positive.

subtopics.title: The Coaching Styles Continuum
subtopics.summary: Five styles (Mosston 1966, adapted by Kirk et al. 1996) from most coach-directed to most participant-directed. No single style is 'best' — match the style to the situation.

sections.heading: The five styles
points: Direct ('show and tell'): coach controls all information and activities; little room for individual needs. E.g. demonstrating a forward roll and having everyone practise the same progression.
Task ('set up and stand back'): different tasks/stations set up to suit different needs; some independent practice while coach circulates giving feedback.
Reciprocal: coach still selects content, but pairs participants (often mixed experience) to give each other feedback — builds both technical and social skills.
Guided discovery ('question and involve'): coach asks open-ended questions to lead participants toward a specific answer (e.g. 'what would happen if you stepped further into your handstand?').
Problem solving: coach sets the problem but accepts varied solutions and no single right answer — participant takes responsibility for finding and testing improvements.

subtopics.title: The Seven BG Coaching Skills
subtopics.summary: What British Gymnastics expects every coach to demonstrate in practice, adjusted for an Assistant Coach's level of responsibility.

sections.heading: Plan & Organise
points: Understand your gymnasts' needs before planning; maximise practice time and minimise queuing.
Arrive on time, correctly dressed, with everything you need and a clear idea of your role.

sections.heading: Build Positive Relationships
points: With gymnasts, other coaches and senior staff — use names, eye contact, smiling, adjusting your physical level, genuine interest.

sections.heading: Use Positive Coaching Behaviours
points: Role model respect, enthusiasm, empathy and trustworthiness — gymnasts learn behaviour through social learning.
Frame mistakes/challenge as growth opportunities, not failure.
Build intrinsic motivation (enjoyment, belonging) rather than relying on external rewards (stickers, treats).
Praise effort, hard work, cooperation and resilience — not only mastered skills.

sections.heading: Effectively Communicate
points: Positive tone of voice with everyone; professional language in line with the Standards of Conduct (no swearing, no slang).
Be an EDI advocate in your language — no assumptions, ask pronouns/preferred names, respect preferences.

sections.heading: Show Safe Skill Development
points: Confirm prerequisite competence before progressing.
Use effective instruction, demonstration, observation and analysis.
Use appropriate progressions in a logical order and physical preparation to support them.
Confidently adapt activities to keep each gymnast optimally challenged.

sections.heading: Show Technical Understanding
points: Technically accurate instructions, demonstrations and feedback.
Combine praise for effort with specific technical detail, e.g. 'good effort using your arms on landing — next time be even stronger with that arm position.'

sections.heading: Create & Maintain Safe & Inclusive Environments
points: Consciously apply all five Foundations of Duty of Care in every session.
Ask yourself: Is everyone safe and included? Are holistic needs met? Am I being an EDI advocate today? Am I within my professional boundaries? Am I gymnast-centred, giving voice and choice?

sections.heading: Evaluate & Reflect
points: Reflect on sessions independently and with your Lead Coach/team.
Identify strengths and development areas and feed them into your CPD plan.
